178: Laches defense to a §256 inventorship correction claim on the '406 patent; presumption of laches applied and not rebutted, so the claim is barred.
Because we agree with the district court's conclusion that the presumption of laches applies against Mr. Lismont's claim and that he failed to rebut that presumption, we affirm.
366: Patent exhaustion defense based on authorized sales under cross-licenses and sublicenses (Alcatel, Nokia Siemens, Ericsson sales); district court held exhaustion barred all infringement claims and the Federal Circuit affirmed.
Accordingly, the judgment of the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey is affirmed.
1271: Equitable estoppel by contract (Cal. Evid. Code § 622) asserted by AngioScore to bar TriReme's inventorship claim; the court rejected the defense.
Estoppel by contract does not apply here, because neither Dr. Lotan nor his successor in interest (TriReme) seeks to enforce any rights under the contract.
1555: License defense: court reaffirmed that certain alleged acts were not licensed under the 2006 license agreement, so the license defense was rejected.
We reaffirm our holdings on the enablement, licensing, and active inducement issues.
2009: Covenant not to sue (license-type defense) held to bar Securus's patent infringement suit because GTL qualifies as an affiliate of PCS under Texas law and the covenant's definition of affiliate includes parent corporations.

the covenant not to sue that Securus entered into as part of the 2009 settlement agreement was applicable to GTL and that the covenant barred Securus from bringing a patent infringement action against GTL before 2014.
2262: Laches defense to pre-suit damages rejected on the equities, including conscious copying
We affirm the rejection of Marvell's laches defense to pre-suit damages.
2336: Section 1498 government-use bar: the court held that 28 U.S.C. § 1498(a) makes the Court of Federal Claims remedy exclusive for indirect infringement claims based on TSA's use of defendants' equipment, requiring dismissal of all three actions.
the statute, within its ambit, makes the remedy against the United States exclusive.
2504: Laches as a defense to legal relief (pre-suit damages) in patent infringement: en banc court held Congress codified laches in 35 U.S.C. 282 and it may bar legal damages notwithstanding 286, so the defense remains available.
Accordingly, we conclude that Congress codified a laches defense in § 282.
2505: Laches and ongoing royalties: absent extraordinary circumstances, laches does not preclude an ongoing royalty for continuing infringement.
absent extraordinary circumstances, laches does not preclude an ongoing royalty.
2506: Equitable estoppel defense at summary judgment: court reinstated the panel's reversal, so the estoppel defense was rejected at this stage.
we reinstate the panel opinion's reversal of the district court's grant of summary judgment on equitable estoppel and adopt its reasoning.
2771: Laches defense to the permanent injunction rejected for lack of reasoned analysis.
Accordingly, the district court did not err in barring the injunction based on Aguila's propounded laches defense.
2816: Assignor estoppel barring Synopsys from challenging the validity of the ’376 patent; summary judgment affirmed.
We affirm the summary judgment that assignor estoppel bars Synopsys from challenging the validity of the ’376 patent.
3035: Exhaustion defense for U.S. domestic sales of Return Program cartridges under a clearly communicated single-use/no-resale restriction: defense rejected, so the restricted sale did not exhaust Lexmark's patent rights (Mallinckrodt reaffirmed).

We conclude that a patentee may preserve its § 271 rights when itself selling a patented article, through clearly communicated, otherwise-lawful restrictions, as it may do when contracting out the manufacture and sale.
3036: Exhaustion defense for cartridges first sold abroad by Lexmark: foreign sale does not exhaust U.S. patent rights (Jazz Photo reaffirmed), so the defense failed.

We also hold that a foreign sale of a U.S.-patented article, when made by or with the approval of the U.S. patentee, does not exhaust the patentee's U.S. patent rights in the article sold, even when no reservation of rights accompanies the sale.
3059: Laches defense to patent infringement damages: district court held Romag's delay constituted laches, reducing the reasonable royalty award; Fed. Cir. held laches remains available under SCA Hygiene and affirmed.
The district court did not err in holding that Fossil could bring a laches defense to a patent infringement claim.
3335: Equitable estoppel barred patentee's infringement suit (license-type defense based on predecessors' silence and conduct, imputed to successor)
We hold that equitable estoppel applies in this instance and High Point is barred from bringing this case against Defendants.
3336: Laches not reached; court declined to address the remaining laches issue
We affirm the district court's judgment and decline to address the remaining issue of laches.
3683: Patent exhaustion defense: the district court's alternative holding that exhaustion applied was vacated because the summary judgment record was insufficiently developed; the court declined to reach exhaustion.
Thus we vacate the district court's ruling with respect to patent exhaustion.
3761: License defense: implied license to the '836 continuation extends to accused AT&T systems, so infringement claims are barred
We agree with the district court, and with AT&T and Ciena, that the licenses include an implied license to the '836 patent that extends to the accused AT&T systems.
4571: Equitable estoppel defense to Ferring's § 256 inventorship-correction claims: the district court granted summary judgment on estoppel, and the Federal Circuit held that the misleading-conduct finding was improper at summary judgment because the Speranza correspondence supports more than one reasonable interpretation, so it vacated and remanded.
In view of the varying reasonable interpretations of the Speranza correspondence, we must vacate the district court's summary judgment of equitable estoppel and remand for further proceedings.
4957: Exhaustion and repair defenses to infringement: sale of F-150 does not exhaust replacement hood and headlamp designs or permit reconstruction
we affirm the district court's ruling that ABPA has not shown that Ford's designs for an F-150 hood and headlamp are exhausted when Ford sells an F-150 truck.
5073: Release defense under the Oyster/Fujitsu settlement agreement, which the court treated as releasing ALU and Cisco from infringement claims on the Fujitsu modulators and receivers; affirmed on the alternative ground that the Fujitsu components substantially embody the claimed invention.
For the reasons that follow, we affirm the decision of the district court on the basis of its alternative ruling.
5427: Assignor estoppel barred accused infringer from challenging validity of '348 patent claim 1 in district court (defense rejected/upheld as applied: estoppel applied)
we affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment of no invalidity as to claim 1 of the '348 patent.
5494: Cisco's assignor estoppel defense; the court held assignor estoppel does not apply in inter partes review, rejecting the defense.
this court held in a concurrently issued opinion that assignor estoppel does not apply in inter partes review proceedings.
5780: Laches defense: laches is no longer a defense to damages within the six-year limitations period under SCA Hygiene; denial of laches defense affirmed.
Because Exmark only seeks damages for the six-year period prior to filing its complaint against Briggs, we agree with the district court that Briggs cannot assert laches as a defense.
6425: Whether assignor estoppel (an equitable estoppel defense to patent validity challenges) bars Arista's IPR challenge. The court held it does not apply in IPR proceedings.
In sum, we conclude that § 311(a), by allowing “a person who is not the owner of a patent” to file an IPR, unambiguously dictates that assignor estoppel has no place in IPR proceedings.
6781: Equitable estoppel defense based on the 2002 demand letter and patentee silence; the district court's estoppel bar was reversed as an abuse of discretion because the reexamined claims did not exist in that form when the letter was sent.
we find that the district court abused its discretion in extending equitable estoppel to the reexamined claims.
6782: Laches defense to damages for infringement within the six-year period under 35 U.S.C. § 286; the court held SCA Hygiene bars the laches defense and reversed the summary judgment on laches.
we hold, and the parties agree, that SCA Hygiene bars Morris's laches defense.
7044: License defense: the 2006 covenant not to sue, treated as a nonexclusive license, bars the infringement claim against Nidec.
For these reasons, we find that the merger clause in the 2007 Settlement does not indicate that the parties intended to revoke the 2006 Covenant.
7566: License defense: the court held that Infinera, as an Affiliate of Coriant, obtained a license under the Licensed Patents under Section 4.1 of the settlement agreement, barring the infringement claims.

Because Infinera is an Affiliate, under Section 4.1 of the Agreement, Oyster has granted Infinera a license under the Licensed Patents, including the patents-in-suit, to make, have made, use, offer for sale, sell, import, export, distribute, or otherwise supply, provide or dispose of, its accused products.
7567: Retroactivity of the license: the court held the license covering products made or sold 'at any time' is retroactive, so it reaches pre-acquisition conduct.
Accordingly, we conclude that Infinera obtained a retroactive license in the patents-in-suit when it became an Affiliate of Coriant.
7612: Settlement and License Agreement with Microsoft (license, release, covenant-not-to-sue) held to cover the accused RadBreadcrumb functionality, barring Caddo's infringement claim against Siemens Industry.
And we conclude, as the district court did, that coverage by § 1.5(b) bars Caddo from succeeding in this infringement case.
8267: License defense: the license agreement with Qualcomm covers the accused products and bars infringement for the period the license was in effect (exhaustion via license).
The license agreement covers subsequent generation products and multi-mode CDMA devices, and therefore precludes infringement for the period that it was in effect.
8334: Equitable estoppel based on GSK's Orange Book and FDA representations was not decided and was left for the district court to try

GSK's representations regarding the Orange Book listing of the '000 patent, Teva's reliance, and fairness go directly to an equitable estoppel defense, which has not yet been tried to the district court.
8450: Whether the covenant not to sue (a license-based defense to AlexSam's breach-of-royalty claim) bars the suit; court held the covenant terminated with the License Agreement, so the defense fails.
Because we hold that the covenant not to sue terminated when the License Agreement terminated, thus allowing AlexSam to sue for failure to pay royalties prior to that time, we reverse and remand.
8717: Equitable intervening rights under 35 U.S.C. § 252 (reexamined patent), an equitable defense to infringement of amended claims; the district court's grant of summary judgment for the accused infringer was affirmed.
we determine that the district court did not abuse its discretion in granting-in-part Morris's motion for summary judgment as to equitable intervening rights.
8735: Assignor estoppel (equitable estoppel-type defense) bars Minerva from challenging the validity of claim 1 of the '348 patent; defense upheld on remand.
we hold that Minerva is estopped from challenging the validity of the '348 patent claims based on the doctrine of assignor estoppel.
9317: Government's license defense under 35 U.S.C. § 202(c)(4) (Bayh-Dole) upheld, defeating the infringement claim; court held the November 1997 subcontract was a funding agreement covering the April 1997 reduction-to-practice work.
We conclude that the provision does apply. We therefore affirm.
10050: License defense: summary judgment that Hilti was licensed and immune from suit under the RectorSeal license, so the infringement claim is barred.
We agree with Hilti that RectorSeal's and Hilti's failure to mark the Inserts did not render the Inserts unlicensed products, and thus that Hilti was not precluded from claiming a License defense.
10105: Prosecution laches in a 35 U.S.C. §145 action: the court held the PTO may assert prosecution laches in a §145 action, that the PTO carried its burden on unreasonable and unexplained delay and prejudice, and that the district court erred in granting Hyatt's Rule 52(c) motion; the laches defense is upheld on the record, with remand for Hyatt to present evidence.
The PTO carried its burden of proving prosecution laches, and the district court erred in granting Hyatt's Rule 52(c) motion for judgment on partial findings.
10705: Prosecution laches, first element: whether PMC's delay in prosecuting the '091 patent was unreasonable and inexcusable under the totality of circumstances; laches defense upheld, rendering the patent unenforceable.
We conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion by legally erring or making clearly erroneous factual findings in determining that Apple established both laches elements.
10706: Prosecution laches, prejudice element: whether Apple suffered prejudice attributable to PMC's delay (intervening rights); laches defense upheld, with the dissent contending Apple showed no prejudice during the period of delay.
We affirm the district court's finding that PMC's delay prejudiced Apple.
10757: Government's license defense under the CRADA based on reduction to practice during the CRADA term; the Court of Federal Claims granted summary judgment for the government, and the Federal Circuit reversed because a genuine fact dispute exists on whether pre-CRADA coupon testing showed the invention worked for its intended purpose, so the license defense was not established at summary judgment.

We hold that the CFC erred in granting summary judgment because a genuine dispute exists as to an issue of material fact—namely, whether a POSA would have known, based on the coupon testing, that the invention would work for its intended purpose.
11647: License defense: partial summary judgment that the Qualcomm license survived termination of the LG-Qualcomm Agreement, so Samsung's Qualcomm-chip products were licensed and not infringing after 2018.
We find that the Qualcomm license survived the Agreement's termination and uphold the district court's grant of partial summary judgment for Samsung's devices with Qualcomm chips.
12325: Equitable estoppel: misleading conduct element. The court agreed the district court correctly found that Fraunhofer's more-than-five-year silence amounted to misleading conduct.

We therefore agree with the district court's conclusion that Fraunhofer's more-than-five-year silence in asserting infringement, in light of its clear knowledge of that infringement, rose to the level misleading conduct.
12326: Equitable estoppel: reliance element. The court held summary judgment improper because SXM did not establish through undisputed evidence that it relied on Fraunhofer's silence, so the estoppel defense failed at summary judgment and the judgment was reversed.
Summary judgment was therefore improper, as SXM has not established through undisputed evidence that it relied on Fraunhofer's misleading conduct.
12436: Prosecution laches defense rejected; the asserted patents were not barred from enforcement.
Therefore, we affirm the Commission’s finding that prosecution laches does not bar Masimo from enforcing its asserted patents.
12534: Prosecution laches defense in a §145 action: court held the defense is available (law of the case) and affirmed judgment for the PTO on prosecution laches, finding no abuse of discretion.
For the foregoing reasons, we affirm the district court's judgment for the PTO on the affirmative defense of prosecution laches.
12676: License defense: whether the RPX patent license agreement and its covenant-not-to-sue barred Lionra's infringement allegations against Cisco's products containing Intel processors.

Thus, because (1) the accused products contain Intel processors, (2) all asserted claims undisputedly require "a processor," and (3) Lionra alleges that the Intel processors satisfy the claimed processor element, we conclude that Lionra's allegations against Cisco are barred by the Agreement.
13931: License defense: whether Aetna's Mastercard Products were licensed (sublicense under License Agreement); court held the license does not cover all alleged infringement and vacated dismissal
Because the district court misconstrued the scope of the license, we must vacate the portion of its judgment dismissing the claims that Aetna infringes with respect to the Mastercard Products.
14331: Whether Sherwin's unilateral covenant not to sue on parent patents created an implied license to PPG for the continuation patents; implied license rejected.
We affirm the district court's finding that Sherwin's Covenant Not to Sue did not create an implied license to the continuation patents.
15158: Prosecution laches as an equitable defense rendering the Zone Scene patents unenforceable; the court held Google failed to prove prejudice, so the defense was rejected.
At bottom, Google presents no evidence that it suffered prejudice attributable to Sonos's delay in claiming, but not disclosing, overlapping zone scenes.
15209: Equitable estoppel defense to cymbal patent infringement claims based on 2011 communications; defense rejected
We cannot say that the district court abused its discretion in denying inMusic's equitable estoppel defense.
